Directions:
Read the following text. Choose the best word(s) for each numbered blank and mark A, B, C or D
on the ANSWER SHEET. (10 points)

Section I Use of English

Text 1

Sleep researchers have long suspected that the brain does something useful at night, but for
decades the evidence remained indirect. The assumption was that sleep simply allowed the body
to rest, and that the brain, being an organ, benefited in the same way a muscle does. That
interpretation began to collapse when recordings from sleeping animals revealed patterns of
activity that looked anything but restful. Certain regions of the brain were firing in
sequences that closely resembled the sequences observed during the day, though compressed and
repeated many times over. The most plausible explanation is that the brain is replaying
experience in order to consolidate it, transferring fragile short-term memories into more
durable storage. If that account is correct, then sleep is not a pause in learning but a
continuation of it by other means. The implication for students is uncomfortable. Staying up
late to revise may feel productive, yet it plausibly undermines the very consolidation the
revision was meant to achieve. Researchers such as Robert Stickgold have argued that the
evidence for this view is now substantial, though they concede that the precise mechanism
remains contested. Not everyone is persuaded. Some sceptics note that replay has been observed
mainly in rodents, and that extrapolating from rats to human learners is a considerable leap.
The dispute is unlikely to be settled soon, but the burden of proof has shifted. The question
is no longer whether sleep contributes to memory, but how much, and under what conditions.

[A] however
[B] therefore
[C] nevertheless
[D] moreover
